title: India's ₹1.5 Lakh Crore Mithai Industry Goes Global as Exports Surge 10 Percent Annually
excerpt: Gulab jamun is now one of the UK's most popular desserts, and Haldiram's ships to North America, Japan and Southeast Asia as demand expands beyond the diaspora.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India's mithai industry is valued at ₹1.5 lakh crore, with exports growing over 10% annually.
  • Gulab jamun is now a top dessert in the UK, expanding beyond Indian communities.
  • The World Mithai and Namkeen Convention 2026 showcased industry advancements and global reach.
  • Innovative packaging technologies are enabling Indian sweets to enter new export markets.

  • India's mithai and namkeen industry is valued at ₹1.5 lakh crore ($18 billion), with exports growing over 10% annually and now accounting for about 10% of production.
  • Indian gulab jamun has become one of the most popular desserts in the United Kingdom, and demand is expanding well beyond diaspora communities to mainstream consumers in Europe, Southeast Asia and North America.
  • The World Mithai and Namkeen Convention (WMNC) 2026 in Hyderabad brought together manufacturers, retailers and technology providers ahead of the festive season.
  • Packaging innovations and longer shelf-life technology have helped Indian sweet makers crack export markets that were previously inaccessible.

Beyond the Diaspora

India's mithai and namkeen industry — valued at nearly ₹1.5 lakh crore — is no longer confined to festive-season domestic consumption. A booming export trade is carrying Indian sweets and savoury snacks to grocery shelves and restaurant menus across four continents, with demand now growing among consumers who have no connection to India at all.

"About 10 per cent of Indian sweets and namkeens are exported, with shipments growing at over 10 per cent annually," Feroz H. Naqvi, Director-General of the Federation of Sweets and Namkeen Manufacturers (FSNM), said on the sidelines of the World Mithai and Namkeen Convention (WMNC) Purchasing 2026 in Hyderabad.

"Hyderabad-based Dadu Mithai Vatika is setting up an exclusive export kitchen to produce motichoor laddus at scale for overseas markets."

The three-day convention, held July 16-18 at the HITEX Exhibition Centre, served as a pre-festive sourcing platform for the industry. It drew manufacturers, retailers, distributors, ingredient suppliers and packaging technology providers from across India, reflecting the scale and sophistication the sector has reached.

Gulab Jamun Conquers the UK

"Indian gulab jamun is now among the most popular desserts in the United Kingdom, while demand is also increasing in Southeast Asian countries," Naqvi told The Hindu BusinessLine. Beyond gulab jamun, rasgulla, soan papdi and Mysore pak are making their way onto dessert menus overseas — including in European markets historically dominated by chocolate confectionery.

"We have been exporting sweets for many decades, but demand has increased considerably of late."

— Neeraj Agarwal, Director, Haldiram's

Haldiram's, the Nagpur-based sweets and namkeen giant, exports to the United States, Canada, Singapore, Japan and Southeast Asian markets. Director Neeraj Agarwal said advances in packaging technology and shelf-life extension have been the key breakthroughs, addressing what were historically the industry's two biggest export barriers.

Building Export Infrastructure

The export momentum is driving investment in dedicated production capacity. Hyderabad-based Dadu Mithai Vatika is setting up an exclusive export kitchen to produce motichoor laddus at scale for overseas markets. The facility is expected to begin operations shortly.

Dadu is also experimenting with chocolate-based Indian sweets and dry-fruit combination products that are gaining particular traction in the Gulf countries, the United States and Europe — a sign that the industry is adapting traditional recipes to suit global palates without losing their essential character.

A Diaspora Connection

For millions of Indians abroad, the expanding availability of authentic mithai is more than a commercial story. Access to familiar sweets during Diwali, Eid, Navratri and other festivals has long been a challenge in cities without large Indian grocery stores. The surge in exports — backed by packaging that preserves quality for weeks rather than days — means an NRI family in a small American town can now order motichoor laddus or kaju katli with the same ease as someone in Mumbai.

The FSNM positioning the convention as "A Perfect Start to the Festive Season" reflects the industry's calendar-driven rhythm. With Navratri, Dussehra and Diwali all falling in the October-November window this year, manufacturers are now locking in ingredients, packaging contracts and export orders months in advance — a level of planning that would have been unusual even a decade ago in what was once a largely informal sector.
